_readme: Seasons + facts for common BD birds, drafted by an agent from cited sources; needs human review.

facts: A largely resident duck of lowland wetlands across the Indian subcontinent; it feeds at night and rests in flocks by day.
It flies slowly with rapid wingbeats, giving a wheezy two-note whistle as flocks circle overhead.
It can perch in trees and sometimes nests in a tree hole or an old kite or heron nest.
It winters in lowland South Asia and flies over the Himalayas to breed on the Tibetan Plateau, crossing the range non-stop in as little as seven hours.
Tracked birds have been recorded as high as 7,290 m.
It waits for the up-valley winds to die down at night and then makes the steepest sustained climbing flights ever recorded for a bird.
One of the largest ducks in the world, found from Africa to South Asia and Indochina.
It nests mainly in tree holes, sometimes in tall grass.
Eastern populations winter in the Indian subcontinent, arriving by October and leaving by April.
Its calls are loud, nasal honks, and males and females sound different.
It often nests far from water, in a tree hole, ruined building, cliff crevice or animal burrow.
Small individuals are the smallest waterfowl on Earth, weighing as little as 160 g.
It nests in tree hollows up to five metres high, and the ducklings leap down to follow their parents to water.
It breeds mainly during the monsoon rains.
Its scientific name querquedula is thought to imitate its call.
The male has a distinctive crackling courtship call; the female is unusually quiet for a duck.
Its genus name Spatula is Latin for 'spoon', after its broad, shovel-like bill.
Birds wintering in the Indian subcontinent make a hard journey over the Himalayas, often resting in wetlands just south of the mountains.
A dabbling duck that dives for food better than its relatives and even steals food from diving birds such as coots.
The female's quack is higher than a mallard's, written as 'gag-ag-ag-ag'.
Unlike most of our ducks, it does not migrate: it lives and breeds in South Asian freshwater wetlands all year.
It is named for the red spot at the base of the bill seen in mainland Indian birds.
Nests on the ground hidden in vegetation near water and lays 8 to 14 eggs.
The drake's long, needle-pointed central tail feathers give the pintail its name.
It breeds across the far north and winters south almost to the equator, including tropical South Asia.
The male's call is a soft 'proop-proop' whistle; the female quacks like a mallard.
One of the smallest dabbling ducks in the world; a drake weighs only about 360 g.
The colour teal is named after this duck.
Its scientific name crecca imitates the male's whistled 'cryc' call.
A diving duck that breeds mainly in Scandinavia and the Siberian steppes and winters farther south.
Although still numerous, it has declined steeply in several regions and is rated Vulnerable by the IUCN.
Also known as the white-eyed pochard: the drake has a striking white eye.
Its scientific name nyroca comes from the Russian word for pochard.
It sometimes builds a floating nest among reeds and other emergent plants.
A Critically Endangered diving duck that breeds in eastern Asia and winters south to Bangladesh and India.
Bangladesh held more than 3,000 Baer's pochards in 1996, a significant share of the world population at the time.
In poor light the male's green-glossed black head can look completely black.
A small diving duck named for the drooping tuft on the back of the drake's head.
Its scientific name fuligula comes from Latin for 'soot' and 'throat'.
The female's call is a harsh, growling 'karr', usually given in flight.
The main wild ancestor of the domestic chicken, native to Bangladesh.
Wild cocks crow a shorter 'cock-a-doodle-doo' than farmyard roosters, cutting off abruptly at the end.
It has different alarm calls for predators in the air and on the ground; only the hens care for the eggs and chicks.
Also called the dabchick, it is the smallest grebe in Europe, Asia and Africa at 23 to 29 cm.
Its breeding call, a trilled 'weet-weet-weet', sounds like a horse whinnying.
Its legs are set so far back that it can barely walk, so it nests at the water's edge and covers its eggs with weed when it leaves.
The wild rock dove is the ancestor of all domestic and city pigeons.
Wild birds nest in crevices on cliffs and rock faces.
Its alarm call at the sight of a predator is a grunting 'oorhh'.
The male has a blue-grey head and a brick-red body; the female is much plainer brown.
Also called the red turtle dove, it is a small pigeon resident in the Asian tropics.
A common resident dove across the Indian subcontinent and East and Southeast Asia.
Look for the black collar patch dotted with white spots on the back and sides of the neck.
It builds a flimsy twig cup, sometimes on buildings, and both parents share building, incubating and feeding.
A widespread resident pigeon of tropical South and Southeast Asia, also called the green-winged pigeon.
Its call is a soft, low moaning of six or seven coos that starts quietly and rises.
It is the state bird of Tamil Nadu in India.
A common green pigeon of the Gangetic Plain and Bangladesh, with bright yellow legs.
Its purple shoulder patch led John Latham to call it the 'purple-shouldered pigeon'.
It is the state bird of Maharashtra in India.
Also called the crow pheasant, it is a big cuckoo that raises its own young and would rather clamber through bushes than fly.
Its booming, low 'coop-coop-coop' is often given as a duet, the female's voice lower than the male's.
An old belief in Bengal held that monocled cobras had no males and mated with greater coucals.
It was first described from a 'lark-heeled cuckoo' from Bengal, hence its scientific name bengalensis; the hind toe has a very long claw.
Its call is a run of low, hollow 'whoot-woot' notes that speed up and drop in pitch.
It builds a domed nest of grass blades low in a tree, mostly after the rains begin.
A cuckoo that raises its own young rather than using other birds' nests.
Waxy bluish-black with a curved green bill and a very long, graduated tail with white tips.
In India its arrival has long been seen as a sign that the monsoon rains are coming.
It is linked with the chataka of Sanskrit poetry, a crested bird that waits for rain to quench its thirst, though in Bengal that name was also given to other birds.
A brood parasite, it lays its egg hurriedly from the rim of the host's nest, often cracking the host's eggs.
A brood parasite: in Bangladesh it lays its eggs mainly in the nests of long-tailed shrikes, common mynas and house crows.
Unusually for a cuckoo, adults feed mainly on fruit, even swallowing hard palm fruits whole.
The male's rising 'koo-Ooo' song fills the air during the breeding season, March to August.
The male's several mournful, whistling calls give the plaintive cuckoo its name.
A brood parasite: it lays its eggs in the nests of cisticolas, prinias and tailorbirds.
Small birds often mob it to chase it away from their nests.
Nicknamed the brainfever bird for its maddening, screaming three-note call that rises in a crescendo before the monsoon.
In Bangla the call is heard as 'চোখ গেল' (chokh gelo), 'my eyes are gone'.
It looks and even flies like a shikra hawk, and lays blue eggs in babblers' nests.
In Bangla its loud call is heard as 'বউ কথা কও' (bou kotha kou), 'wife, please speak'.
A brood parasite that lays one egg, mostly in drongo and crow nests, after removing and eating one of the host's eggs.
The male distracts the hosts while the female slips in to lay; some populations move south in winter.
A resident nightjar whose mottled plumage makes it almost invisible against leaf litter.
Its territorial song is a long, monotonous series of notes given at night.
The female builds no nest, laying one or two eggs straight onto the leaf litter on the ground.
A common resident swift of tropical Asia, closely tied to palm trees.
It glues its nest of down and feathers to the underside of a palm leaf with saliva, and even glues its eggs in place.
Also called the waterhen, it is one of the most common rails of the Old World.
Females sometimes lay eggs in other moorhens' nests, and even in the nests of other species.
It makes all sorts of gargling calls and hisses loudly when threatened.
A slaty-black waterbird with a white bill and white forehead shield.
It bobs its head as it swims and dives with a little jump.
Noisy, with crackling, explosive and trumpeting calls, often at night.
A big blue-purple swamphen, 43 cm long, with a pale grey head and a stout red bill.
In courtship the male bows to the female holding water weeds in his bill, chuckling loudly.
It was split from the purple swamphen as a full species in 2015.
The only member of its genus, a rail of wet grassland and paddy fields.
It is noisy at dawn and dusk with a loud, gulping call.
It nests on dry ground in marsh vegetation, laying 3 to 6 eggs.
In Bangla it is the dahuk (ডাহুক), a familiar voice of village ponds.
Bolder than most rails, it walks slowly with its tail cocked, even in drains beside busy roads.
It calls loudly and croakily, especially at dawn and dusk and after the first rains.
One of Asia's rarest waterbirds: a 2020 study suggested the world population may be only 100 to a few hundred birds.
Known breeding populations survive at only four sites, in Bangladesh and Cambodia; in Bangladesh it breeds from June to September.
It builds a pad of small sticks low above water, and the chicks leave the nest soon after hatching.
A large, big-eyed wader with a massive, upturned bill; its scientific name means 'backward-bent bill'.
It lives on gravel banks along big rivers, lakes and beaches, laying a single egg in a bare scrape on open shingle.
Its wailing whistle is given mainly at night.
A black-and-white wader with extremely long pink legs and a thin black bill.
Some populations migrate to the coasts in winter, while those in warmer regions are mostly resident.
It breeds in Siberia and Alaska and flies south to Asia, Australasia and Pacific islands from August–September to April–May.
Tracked birds have flown 4,800 km non-stop from Alaska to Hawaii in three to four days.
Most wintering birds feed alone within their own territory.
It breeds in northeast China and Japan; the mainland population winters from northeastern India to Cambodia.
Its call is a sharp 'chee-it'.
Its loud alarm call, rendered 'did-he-do-it', warns of any person or animal moving nearby, by day or night.
Like other lapwings it cannot perch in trees.
It has even nested between the rails of a railway track, leaving the eggs each time a train passed.
A small plover that breeds in East Asia and winters on coasts including Indian beaches, often in mixed flocks with its look-alikes.
It was recently split from the Tibetan sand plover; together they used to be called the lesser sand plover.
It nests in a bare scrape on the ground, laying three eggs.
A small migratory plover; look for the bright yellow ring around its eye.
It nests right on bare stony or gravelly ground near fresh water, with little or no plant cover.
A role-reversed bird: the bigger, brighter female courts several males, and the males incubate the eggs and raise the young.
Linnaeus named it from a picture of a 'Bengall water rail' sent from Bengal, hence benghalensis.
Very long toes and claws let it walk across floating leaves on lakes and beels.
It is the only jacana with different breeding and non-breeding plumages; outside the breeding season the golden nape almost disappears.
The female builds the nest on floating vegetation; its typical call is a mewing 'me-onp'.
Females are polyandrous, keeping a harem of males during the monsoon breeding season.
Males carry and brood chicks under their wings, which may be helped by a flattened wing bone.
Eggs are sometimes laid straight onto a floating lotus leaf.
Its name 'whimbrel' imitates its rippling, whistled call.
The eastern race breeds in north-eastern Siberia and winters from India to Australia.
The largest wading bird in its range; in Scotland it is called the 'whaup'.
Its name 'curlew' imitates its call.
Breeds from Iceland across Europe and Central Asia and migrates in flocks to places including South Asia.
The name 'godwit', first recorded around 1416, is believed to imitate its call, a strident 'weeka weeka weeka'.
It is named after the frilly Elizabethan ruff collar, because breeding males grow showy neck ruffs and head tufts; females are called reeves.
Some males are permanent female mimics called 'faeders', the first such males known in any bird.
Highly gregarious, it can form huge flocks on its wintering grounds, which include southern Asia.
One of the world's rarest waders, it breeds on the Bering Sea coast and winters in South and Southeast Asia, including Bangladesh.
Its most distinctive feature is its spatulate, spoon-shaped bill.
It is Critically Endangered: in 2016 the world population was estimated at only 240 to 456 mature birds.
One of the smallest waders, weighing only 21 to 51 g.
It breeds in north-east Russia and spends the non-breeding season on the coasts of Southeast Asia and Australasia.
Shy and well camouflaged, it hides close to the ground and flushes only when approached closely.
In courtship the male dives through the air, making a 'drumming' sound with vibrating tail feathers.
Named after the Terek River near the Caspian Sea, where it was first observed.
It breeds in the Siberian taiga and winters on tropical coasts including South Asia, preferring muddy areas.
A small Palearctic wader of river banks, pond edges and coasts; in winter plumage it is duller, with faint barring on the wings.
It and its American twin, the spotted sandpiper, replace each other geographically, and strays sometimes pair up and hybridise.
Its scientific name nebularia comes from Latin for 'mist', referring to its damp marshy habitat.
Its usual call is three short, fluty notes: 'teu-teu-teu'.
It winters in Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Australasia, usually on fresh water.
An Endangered wader of the East Asian–Australasian Flyway that winters in Bangladesh and Southeast Asia.
Unusually for a sandpiper, it can nest up in larch trees, building with larch twigs lined with lichen.
The smallest of the shanks, a freshwater wader that winters in Africa, South Asia and Australia.
It nests on the ground, or sometimes reuses an old tree nest of a thrush such as a fieldfare.
Wary and loud, it alerts other birds with its piping call.
It winters on coasts in South Asia among other places.
It breeds on the high plateaus of Central Asia and winters on the coasts and big inland lakes of the Indian subcontinent.
It nests on the ground in colonies in reedbeds, marshes or lake islands, and is highly gregarious in winter.
Easily the world's largest black-headed gull, and the third-largest gull of any kind.
Its scientific name means 'fish eagle' in Greek.
It breeds in Central Asia and winters south to India.
A small tern; the Asian subspecies sinensis is resident on the river systems of northern India and eastward.
It fiercely defends its nest and young, attacking intruders.
Its call is a loud, distinctive creaking.
The world's largest tern, with a wingspan of up to 145 cm.
Its name refers to the Caspian Sea.
It nests on bare ground among gravel and sand, alone or in colonies.
The largest of the marsh terns; tropical birds are resident while Asian breeders winter south to the Indian subcontinent.
Pallas thought it might be a hybrid of two other terns, hence its scientific name hybrida.
A resident tern of big inland rivers, almost never seen on salt water.
It lays three blotched eggs in a scrape on bare sand or rock.
It has become very rare in the east of its range, in China, Cambodia, Laos and Thailand.
Its lower bill is longer than the upper and is ploughed through the water as it flies low over rivers.
India and Bangladesh are the last strongholds of this declining species.
It nests in a scrape on open sandbanks and sometimes lays eggs in river terns' nests.
Widespread and common in Bangladesh; adults have a gap between the arched upper and curved lower bill.
Young birds are born without the gap, which forms only with age.
A bird ringed in Thailand was found 1,500 km to the west in Bangladesh.
A tall, black-and-white stork with a heavy bill; males and females differ in eye colour, which is rare among storks.
It is exceedingly rare in Bangladesh and may no longer breed here.
A big bald-headed stork that keeps to wetlands and fields and scavenges less than the greater adjutant.
In 2011 a small colony of about 6 nests and 20 birds was found near Thakurgaon in Bangladesh.
Mostly silent, it clatters its bill, hisses and moans at the nest.
Its Bangla name hargila is said to come from Sanskrit for 'bone swallower'.
Once widespread, it was recorded breeding in the Sundarbans in the 1850s, but the IUCN considers it probably extinct in Bangladesh.
Its wingspan averages 250 cm, making it a rival for the largest stork in the world.
Named for the pink feathers on the adults' back.
It sweeps its half-open bill through the water and snaps it shut on fish it senses by touch.
Mostly silent like other storks, it clatters its bill at the nest.
It swims with its body underwater and only its thin neck showing, which earns it the name snakebird.
It spears fish underwater, then tosses and juggles them at the surface before swallowing them head first.
It nests in mixed heronries, building stick platforms in trees usually standing in water.
A small cormorant of ponds, lakes and streams; a study in Bangladesh found it breeds from May to October.
When it surfaces to swallow a fish, other birds, including other cormorants, storks, gulls and egrets, try to steal it.
It nests in colonies beside pond herons and little egrets, sometimes on coconut palms.
Called the large cormorant in India; it ties for the second-largest cormorant in the world.
Pairs reuse the same nest site year after year.
The smallest pelican in its region, told by the dark spots on the upper bill, which appear only after the first year.
Fishermen in eastern Bengal once used it as a decoy for certain fish.
Reports of it in Bangladesh have been questioned; it breeds only in peninsular India, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.
A small, chestnut-coloured bittern of tropical and subtropical Asia, mostly resident.
When surprised, it freezes in the classic bittern pose, called the 'on-guard'.
A tall heron that hunts by standing motionless beside or in the water, or stalking slowly through the shallows.
Its main call is a loud, croaking 'fraaank'.
Resident in much of its range, but northern populations migrate south in autumn.
Slimmer and darker than the grey heron, it weighs only 0.5 to 1.35 kg despite its size.
Tropical Asian populations are mainly sedentary.
It is more secretive than the grey heron, and its harsh 'frarnk' call is quieter and higher-pitched.
A large egret, only slightly smaller than the grey heron.
It builds tree nests in colonies close to water; the male chooses the site and starts the nest before attracting a female.
Despite its name it is not an Egretta egret: it sits in the genus Ardea with the great herons.
A slim white heron with a slender black bill and long black legs.
It nests in colonies with other wading birds, on stick platforms in trees, bushes, reed beds or bamboo clumps.
Both parents incubate the three to five bluish-green eggs for about three weeks.
It follows cattle and other large animals, snapping up the insects and small creatures they disturb.
It uses drier, more open habitats than other herons, which helped it spread across much of the world.
Its species name ibis was applied by mistake; it originally referred to the sacred ibis.
Also called the paddybird, it stalks the edges of ponds and paddies all over South Asia.
Its streaky camouflage lets people walk right up to it, which gave rise to folk beliefs that it is short-sighted or blind.
When it takes off, bright white wings suddenly flash from its drab brown body.
A small, mostly sedentary heron also called the mangrove heron.
It sometimes fishes with bait, dropping a feather or leaf on the water and grabbing the fish that come to look.
Often just called the night heron; it is found across most of the world.
Very noisy at its nesting colonies, with calls written as 'quok' or 'woc'.
It nests in colonies on stick platforms in groups of trees or in reed beds.
Like storks, it has no true voice and is silent apart from grunts made by pairs at the nest.
It nests only in the rainy season, in mixed heronry colonies near wetlands.
It is the only native all-white ibis in its range with a black head and neck.
A white wader with a flat, spoon-shaped bill.
Northern breeders migrate south for the winter, while populations in warmer parts of Asia stay put or move locally.
In England it was once called the 'shovelard'.
A fish-eating raptor found on every continent except Antarctica.
It is an uncommon to fairly common winter visitor to all parts of South Asia; a bird tagged in Norway was tracked to western India.
A small raptor best known for hovering over open grassland like a kestrel.
It builds a loose twig platform and lays 3 or 4 eggs; the female does most of the nest building.
Once numbered in the millions; now Critically Endangered, with fewer than 6,000 mature birds worldwide in 2021.
It is killed by kidney failure after eating carcasses of livestock treated with the painkiller diclofenac.
It nests in tall trees, often near villages in Bangladesh and India, laying a single egg.
A forest eagle that hunts snakes and lizards, often near wet grassland.
Size varies unusually much across its many subspecies, from the Himalayas to Southeast Asia.
Its plumage varies from pale to dark with age and moult, giving it the name 'changeable'.
The most widespread, adaptable and abundant hawk-eagle in its genus, it hunts birds, mammals and reptiles in forest.
It hunts by gliding low over open ground with its wings held in a shallow V and its legs often dangling.
The genus name Circus comes from Greek kirkos, 'circle', for its circling flight.
Some breeding birds migrate to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar for the winter.
A small hawk, also called the little banded goshawk; its call is a 'pee-wee' with a higher first note and a longer second.
Drongos mimic its calls, apparently to scare other birds off their food so they can steal it.
The Indian subspecies dussumieri, found in Bangladesh, is resident on the plains and lower hills.
Thought to be the world's most abundant member of the hawk and eagle family, with up to 6.7 million birds.
An opportunistic scavenger; it has even been seen tearing apart baya weaver nests to get at the eggs or chicks.
Northern birds migrate to South Asia in winter, joining the resident Indian race; its call is a shrill whistle followed by a rapid whinny.
A familiar, resident kite of Bangladesh, with a reddish-brown body and white head and breast.
Mainly a scavenger of dead fish and crabs, it also steals prey from other birds.
Both parents build the nest, often in mangroves.
An Endangered fish eagle that breeds from Central Asia to India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
In Bangladesh its prey includes rohu, catla, mrigal carp and even ilish.
It is partially migratory: Central Asian birds spend the winter among the resident birds of northern South Asia.
A big white-and-grey eagle found regularly along the coasts of Bangladesh.
Pairs often honk in unison, a loud goose-like call that carries a long way.
Some nest sites are used continuously for many years; one in Australia was occupied for over fifty years.
A large fish-eating eagle that is uncommon and local in Bangladesh.
It builds a huge stick nest, up to 1.5 m across and, with repeated use, up to 2 m deep.
It is easily confused with the lesser fish eagle and Pallas's fish eagle.
It hunts by flying slowly and quartering the ground, hovering over spots that might hide prey.
Rodents make up the largest share of its food.
Before she starts laying, the female is fed entirely by the male.
A small owl with ear tufts, resident from northern Pakistan and India to Bangladesh and southern China.
It is nocturnal, but small birds often give away its daytime roost by mobbing it.
It nests in tree hollows, laying 3 to 5 eggs.
The most widespread and common of the four fish owls, resident across the Indian subcontinent.
Unlike fish-eating hawks, it does not plunge in: it snatches fish with its feet or wades into the shallows on foot.
A common little owl of farmland and villages that has adapted to life in cities.
Small birds mob it in daytime, which often gives away where it is perched.
Its call is a harsh, loud churring and chuckling 'chirurr-chirurr-chirurr'.
Its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call may be the origin of both its English and scientific names.
Cinnamon-coloured, with a tall crest, black-and-white wings and a long, curved bill.
The nesting female and chicks can make a foul-smelling liquid to deter predators.
A huge forest hornbill, listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN since 2018.
The female seals herself into a tree hollow with a plaster made mostly of droppings, and is fed through a slit while she nests.
Pairs call in unison, building to a rapid mix of roars and barks; one has lived nearly 50 years in captivity.
One of the smallest and most common Asian hornbills, with the widest range in its genus.
The female seals herself inside a tree cavity with a mix of saliva, mud, fruit, droppings and bark, leaving only a slit for food to be passed in.
Its calls range from crow-like sounds to braying, harsh crackles and screeches.
A sparrow-sized kingfisher with blue upperparts and orange underparts that dives for fish.
In the tropics it lives by slow rivers, mangrove creeks and swamps, such as those of Bangladesh.
Its flight call is a short, sharp whistled 'chee', repeated two or three times.
A big kingfisher found only along the north and east coasts of the Bay of Bengal, from Bangladesh to Thailand.
It lives in mangrove forest; in India it is mainly known from the Sundarbans.
A big kingfisher with a heavy bill that hunts fish, frogs, crabs, rodents and even young birds.
Its far-carrying call is a low 'peer-por-por' repeated about every five seconds.
It digs its nest in river banks, rotting trees or tree termite nests, and stays in the same area all year.
A rust-red kingfisher with a very large, bright red bill and red legs.
It lives in thick forest, so its high, descending call is heard far more often than the bird is seen.
Its scientific name recalls the Coromandel Coast of India.
Often found far from water, it eats reptiles, frogs, crabs, rodents and even small birds.
In Bengali it is called the sada-buk machhranga, the 'white-breasted kingfisher'.
To start a nest, the pair fly straight into a mud bank until they make a dent, then dig a tunnel with their bills.
A striking kingfisher with a black cap, white throat, purple-blue wings and a coral-red bill.
It is the most northerly of the tree kingfishers; northern populations migrate south for the winter.
Its call is a cackling 'ki-ki-ki-ki-ki'.
Also called the mangrove kingfisher; local subspecies live along the coasts of India and Bangladesh.
Its typical call is a loud, harsh, metallic 'kee-kee-kee'.
It lays its eggs straight onto the floor of a burrow in a rotten tree, termite nest or earth bank, with no nest material.
A black-and-white kingfisher that hovers over water before diving bill-first for fish.
Males have two breast bands, females a single broken one.
It digs a nest tunnel 4 to 5 feet long into a vertical mud bank.
A small green bee-eater resident in the lowlands of South Asia, increasingly common in towns.
It hunts from low perches, often launching from wires or TV antennas in a zigzag flight to snatch an insect.
It nests in tunnels dug into vertical mud banks.
Many populations are strongly migratory and breed in colonies, mostly in river valleys.
It digs a nest tunnel up to nearly 2 m long into a sandy bank.
It calls mainly in flight with a rolling, chirping 'teerp'.
Its wings flash brilliant light and dark blue in flight; in breeding displays it rolls through the air with harsh 'kaarsch' calls.
In Bengal, seeing one was a good omen: people chanted a couplet to Vishnu, wishing to see the bird at the time of their death.
It boldly drives off crows from its nest and has even been seen dive-bombing vultures and people.
Its metronomic 'tuk…tuk…tuk' sounds like a coppersmith beating copper sheet, which gives it its name.
It carves its own nest hole in dead wood and also uses holes for roosting.
Red-vented bulbuls sometimes rob the male of berries he brings to the nest.
Its green plumage blends into the canopy, so its loud calls are often the only sign it is there.
It repeats its 'took-a-rook' call 90 to 105 times a minute.
Both parents dig the nest hole in a tree trunk and raise the young.
One of the few woodpeckers often seen in towns, with a rattling, whinnying call and bouncing flight.
It is the only golden-backed woodpecker with both a black throat and a black rump.
It appears on a 3.75 Taka postage stamp from Bangladesh.
A small falcon that spots prey and drops on it in a short, steep dive.
Northern birds winter south of the breeding range, including northeastern India.
It nests in holes in cliffs, trees or buildings and often reuses old crow nests.
One of the largest parakeets, 56 to 62 cm long, and uncommon in Bangladesh.
It is named after Alexander the Great, who is said to have taken many of these birds from Punjab to Europe.
Its calls are deeper and harsher than those of the rose-ringed parakeet.
Native to the Indian subcontinent and tropical Africa, it has set up feral populations around the world after escaping from the pet trade.
A noisy parakeet with an unmistakable squawk.
It picks and defends nest holes in the cool season, and the young leave the nest before the monsoon.
A tiny green parrot only 14 cm long, with a short tail; the male has a red rump and bill.
It wanders locally following fruit, seeds and blossoms, visiting banyan figs and banana flowers for nectar.
It nests in tree cavities lined with bits of leaves.
Called navrang or nauranga, 'nine colours', in parts of India; in Bengali it is the shumcha.
Shy despite its colours, it gives a distinctive two-note whistle at dawn and dusk.
It breeds during the south-west monsoon, building a ball-shaped nest with a side entrance on or near the ground.
A colourful pitta of mangroves, found from Bangladesh and India to Malaysia and Indonesia.
Unlike most pittas, it is fairly easy to see because it perches high in mangrove trees to call.
Its call, written 'wieuw-wieuw', is more slurred than that of the blue-winged pitta.
A bright yellow oriole with a black hood, resident across tropical southern Asia; Bengal is its type locality.
A Bengali folk tale says a merchant's wife, tortured by her mother-in-law, was brought back by a goddess as this bird, so it is called benebou ('merchant's wife').
It is also called haldi pakhi, the 'turmeric bird'.
Widespread in Bangladesh, usually seen perched in tight groups on power lines, bare trees or palms.
It often nests at the base of a palm frond, or even in a hollow on top of a street-light post.
Its wheezy song can include imitations of other birds.
Easy to find by its loud whistles; the song is a trilled 'wheeeee-tee'.
In the breeding season the male fluffs up and spirals through the air like a green, black, yellow and white ball.
It builds a neat cup of grass bound with cobwebs in the fork of a tree.
A glossy black bird with a deeply forked tail, a common resident in Bangladesh; in Bengali it is the finge.
Only 28 cm long, it fearlessly attacks much bigger birds, including crows and birds of prey, that enter its nesting territory.
In Hindi it is called kotwal, 'policeman'; one of its calls imitates the shikra.
Its two long outer tail feathers are bare shafts with 'rackets' only at the tips.
A brilliant mimic, it learns and copies the alarm calls of other birds in mixed feeding flocks.
In most of its Asian range it is the largest drongo.
Adult males grow drooping central tail streamers up to 30 cm long; some males are rufous while others are white.
It has resident and breeding populations in most of Bangladesh.
Pairs sometimes nest near drongos, which keep predators away; the nest is a neat cup of twigs and spider webs.
It breeds from Mongolia to Siberia and winters in South Asia, Myanmar and the Malay Peninsula, setting up winter territories soon after it arrives.
Lanius is Latin for 'butcher': shrikes are known as butcher birds for the way they treat their prey.
When it sings it keeps its bill closed, so only its throat pulses.
Its scientific name schach imitates its call, and 'shrike' comes from Old English for 'shriek'.
In Bangladesh it is one of the hosts of the Asian koel and other parasitic cuckoos.
It often perches on roadside wires, watching for prey.
A long-tailed, rusty-brown member of the crow family with loud, musical calls, common in gardens and farmland.
Its common 'ko-tree' or 'bob-o-link' call gives it the local name kotri; another name is taka chor, 'coin thief'.
Like other crows it is omnivorous and opportunistic.
Described in 1817 from a specimen collected in Bengal, it has since spread around the world on ships.
It is the only crow known to pass the mirror test of self-recognition in a laboratory.
It nests in trees, sometimes several nests to a tree, and occasionally on telephone towers.
Formerly called the jungle crow, it is named for its heavy bill: macrorhynchos is Greek for 'long-billed'.
Extremely adaptable, it can eat almost anything and colonise new areas, so it is often seen as a nuisance.
It builds a twig platform nest high up in a tree.
Famous for sewing leaves together around its nest, it appears as Darzee in Kipling's Jungle Book.
In Bangla it is the tuntuni, and Upendrakishore Ray's classic children's folk-tale book 'Tuntunir Boi' is named after it.
Shy and hidden in foliage, it gives itself away with a loud 'cheeup-cheeup-cheeup'.
A small, plain wren-warbler that is a resident breeder from Pakistan and India to south China and Southeast Asia.
It builds its nest in a shrub or tall grass and lays three to six eggs.
A tiny grassland warbler named for the regular 'zit' calls the male gives during his zigzagging display flight.
The male builds the first frame of the nest deep in the grass, then invites females with a special display.
It was formerly called the fan-tailed warbler.
A small brown martin of open farmland and grassland, usually near water.
It was formerly treated as part of the plain martin, now called the brown-throated martin.
The most widespread swallow in the world, found on every continent, with vagrants even in Antarctica.
One subspecies breeds in Siberia and winters from eastern Bengal to Thailand and Malaysia.
It has separate alarm calls: a sharp 'siflitt' for cats and a 'flitt-flitt' for hawks.
One of our commonest garden birds; elsewhere it is on the list of the world's 100 worst invasive species.
Its typical call has been written as 'ginger beer', and many other birds heed its alarm calls.
It has nested in odd places, including on floating water hyacinth and inside a bus in regular use.
A crested bulbul with a red 'whisker' patch, common in hill forests and gardens.
Its loud call is a sharp 'kink-a-joo', also written as 'pleased to meet you'.
It often calls from treetops in the morning.
A skulking leaf warbler that breeds in the eastern Palearctic and winters in South and Southeast Asia.
In winter its harsh 'check' call is often the first clue that it is hiding in nearby bushes or reeds.
A small yellow-green bird with a bright white eye-ring, described in 1824 from a Bengal specimen.
Highly sociable, it forages in small groups for nectar and insects, rarely coming down to the ground.
It hangs a compact cup nest of cobwebs, lichen and plant fibre like a hammock in the fork of a branch.
It moves about in noisy groups of six to ten, which is why it is called 'seven sisters' in northern India and 'seven brothers' in Bengali.
Groups defend territories, mob snakes and other predators together, and groom and play-fight with each other.
It is a common resident across most of the subcontinent, first described from Bengal specimens in 1823.
Famous as a talking cage bird, it is now virtually extinct in Bangladesh because of forest loss and the pet trade.
Each bird has 3 to 13 call types, learned when young, and birds more than 15 km apart share none.
Its calls include whistles, wails, screeches and gurgles, often eerily human-like.
A black-and-white myna found in small groups across the Gangetic plains and Bangladesh.
It builds a messy domed nest of straw with a side entrance, often in a banyan, mango or jackfruit tree near people.
Linnaeus named it from a 'Contra, from Bengall', though the Bengali name 'contra' was later unknown.
Native to South Asia including Bangladesh, it has spread so fast elsewhere that the IUCN lists it among the world's 100 worst invasive species.
Before settling into communal roosts, flocks call together in a din known as 'communal noise'.
Its repertoire includes croaks, squawks, chirps, clicks, whistles and growls, often delivered with fluffed feathers and bobbing head.
Named for its habit of nesting almost only in burrows it digs into earthen riverbanks and embankments, often in big colonies.
It looks like a common myna but has brick-red, not yellow, bare skin behind the eye.
A noisy bird whose calls range from clucks and croaks to screeches, whistles and warbles.
A common resident myna of Bangladesh, recognised by the tuft of feathers on its forehead.
It was first described from Bengal in 1827.
It sometimes lines its nest hole with shed snake skins.
The national bird of Bangladesh, known as the doyel (দোয়েল).
It appears on a Bangladeshi currency note, and Doel Chattar (Doel Square) in Dhaka is named after it.
Famous for its song, it nests in tree hollows or niches in walls and buildings and readily uses nest boxes.
It breeds in boggy birch woods and swamps from Europe to western Alaska and winters in southern Asia, including the Indian subcontinent.
Besides the male's blue throat, look for the tail: brown with rusty-red patches at the base.
It breeds in the eastern Palearctic and the Himalayas and winters in the Old World tropics.
The male's call is a click like two pebbles knocked together.
The tiny male has a bright scarlet stripe running down his back from crown to tail.
It weaves a pouch-shaped nest with a side entrance, hung from a branch high in a tree.
A common resident sunbird of Bangladesh, southern India and Sri Lanka.
The female alone builds a hanging pouch nest of cobwebs and plant fibres, studded outside with lichen, bark and seeds.
Males are told from purple sunbirds by their pale underparts.
It can hover like a hummingbird to sip nectar, though it usually perches at the base of the flower.
In harsh sunlight the male can look all black; the purple sheen shows in good light.
It sometimes steals nectar by slitting flowers open at the base.
A long-billed nectar feeder of moist forests; unlike most sunbirds, males and females look alike.
It hangs its hammock-like nest under a banana leaf with about 150 'pop-rivets' of cobweb and plant fibre, a unique use of spider silk.
The babui (বাবুই) of Bangla, famous for its hanging, retort-shaped nests often hung from palm fronds.
Males weave the nests from strips of paddy leaves, grasses and palm fronds, making up to 500 trips per nest.
A long vertical entrance tube leads up to the nest chamber, keeping predators out.
In Bangla it is the kalo-buk babui (কালোবুক বাবুই), the 'black-breasted weaver'.
The male builds the nest alone; females visit late in construction, tugging and testing it before choosing a mate.
His soft courtship song sounds like a cricket or a squeaky, unoiled bicycle wheel.
A tiny finch whose breeding males turn strawberry-red; it breeds in the monsoon.
Both its scientific name and 'avadavat' come from Ahmedabad, the Indian city from which caged birds were exported.
It builds a ball-shaped nest of grass blades.
A common munia named for the scale-like markings on its breast and belly; the pet trade calls it the nutmeg mannikin.
The male's song is so soft it can only be heard close by.
In courtship, a bird holding nest material flies around in a zigzag path.
A small bird that lives alongside people across most of the world.
Most of its calls are variations on a short chirp, used by males to claim a nest and invite a mate.
Females and young are plain brown and grey; males have bolder black, white and brown markings.
Many populations breed in Eurosiberia and migrate to tropical Asia and Africa for the winter.
In winter it often feeds along roadsides, flushing with a sharp 'chi-cheep', flying ahead and then circling back.
Breeding males have a black throat; the yellow underneath is limited to the throat and vent.
Like all wagtails it constantly wags its long tail; most populations migrate to tropical Africa and southern Asia for the winter.
Breeding males are olive above and yellow below, and the call is a high-pitched 'jeet'.
A small wagtail of wet meadows and bogs that migrates to South Asia for the winter.
Its scientific name citreola is Latin for 'lemon yellow', after its colouring.
Asiatic white wagtails migrate to the Middle East, India and Southeast Asia for the winter.
As many as six subspecies may winter together in India and Southeast Asia, which makes them tricky to tell apart.
Its call is a sharp 'chissick'.
One of the few pipits that breeds in South Asia; it is non-migratory.
In the breeding season it sings by repeating a note as it drops from a short, fluttering flight.
Its usual call is a 'chip-chip-chip', quite different from the winter-visiting pipits.
Once abundant, it has crashed since the early 2000s and is now Critically Endangered.
The decline is blamed mainly on heavy trapping during migration and on the wintering grounds, especially in China.
It breeds from Finland to the Bering Sea and winters in southern and southeastern Asia, including India.
